title: BITS Jobs
summary: BITS jobs abuse the Windows Background Intelligent Transfer Service, a component that downloads and uploads files asynchronously in the background using spare bandwidth. Jobs are created through the Component Object Model interface, which is reachable from PowerShell, from the bitsadmin command line tool, and from ordinary programs, so an intruder does not need to drop a new executable. A job holds a queue of file operations; it can pull a payload from a remote server, run a program when the transfer completes or errors, and remain defined for a long period, since the default maximum job lifetime is measured in months and can be extended. Persistence follows from that behaviour: a long-lived job, or a completion command, can re-trigger after a reboot because the service restarts with Windows. The same upload capability moves data out to an attacker-controlled server. Detection leans on the BITS operational event log, on command lines that reference bitsadmin or the Start-BitsTransfer PowerShell cmdlet, on unusual destinations in transfer records, and on jobs whose owner or timing does not match any software management tool.

beginner.definition: BITS is a Windows service that moves files in the background while you work. Attackers can use it to download their tools and start them later. The service does the work quietly and is already trusted by the system. It is a way to fetch and run files without writing obvious new programs.
beginner.whyItMatters: BITS is a normal part of Windows, so security tools rarely block it. A job can be set to wait and then run a program, even after a restart. Jobs live in the service database, so there may be no new file or registry entry to find. If you never look at BITS activity, an attacker can download tools and stay resident without much noise.
howItWorks: The attacker creates a BITS job through PowerShell, the bitsadmin tool or a program using the COM interface.
The job is given one or more file transfers, for example downloading a file to a folder on the computer.
BITS performs the transfer in the background using spare bandwidth, which looks like normal update traffic.
The attacker adds a command that should run when the job finishes or fails.
A job can be created with a long lifetime, so the transfer or command can occur again after a reboot.
The upload direction is also available, so the same service can send files out of the network.
beginner.example: Think of a courier service that is already allowed into your building. Staff wave it through because it delivers office supplies every day. A thief fills in the same paperwork and uses the courier to move boxes out of the back door. Nothing was forced and the guard saw a familiar uniform. The sign of trouble is a delivery that no department ordered.
takeaways: A long-running BITS job can act as a repeated download and execution channel.
Look at BITS job records, their owner, destination and any completion command.
Strange outbound file transfers can be exfiltration, even when the service is trusted.

objectives: Describe what the Background Intelligent Transfer Service does and why programs use it.
Explain how a BITS job can download, execute and clean up files on a host.
Explain how a long-lived job or completion command provides persistence across reboots.
Identify the Windows BITS operational log and command line artefacts that reveal job creation.
Distinguish legitimate software update transfers from suspicious BITS job ownership and destinations.
